claims.text: Cold rolling followed by annealing will produce a uniform, fine-grained HfZrTiTa0.53 microstructure.
The resulting fine-grained microstructure will enhance dislocation-mediated strain hardening.
The intervention will improve tensile ductility and uniform elongation in HfZrTiTa0.53.
The intervention will preserve the alloy's high yield strength.
The intervention will preserve impact-triggered energy release.
As-produced HfZrTiTa0.53 has a yield strength of 786 MPa.
As-produced HfZrTiTa0.53 has a compressive strength of 1314 MPa.
The reported 13.5% terminal strain represents limited tensile ductility in HfZrTiTa0.53.
As-produced HfZrTiTa0.53 has suboptimal load-bearing reliability.
A moderate cold-rolling reduction of approximately 5–10% followed by annealing is the proposed processing intervention.
An annealing temperature of approximately 600–700°C is likely to retain strength without degrading impact energy release.
The resulting microstructure will have a higher density of mobile dislocations.
Grain refinement will promote uniform plastic deformation by enhancing dislocation accumulation and delaying necking.
Cold rolling introduces dislocation structures that evolve into fine, uniform grains during controlled annealing.
Uniform elongation will increase from 13.5% to approximately 20% or more.
The processed alloy will retain a yield strength near or above 750 MPa.
Impact-triggered energy release will remain similar to that of the unprocessed control.
The proposed benefits are applicable at room temperature under quasi-static tensile strain rates of approximately 10^-3 to 10^-1 s^-1.

contradictions.description: The 13.5% value is described as terminal tensile strain but is then used as though it were the baseline uniform elongation; terminal strain and uniform elongation are not interchangeable measurements.
An increase from 13.5% to 20.0% is about 48%, not the stated minimum 50% relative improvement; a 50% increase would require at least 20.25%.

The predicted yield-strength floor is approximately 750 MPa, but the falsification rule permits losses up to 10% from 786 MPa, corresponding to about 707 MPa. Results between about 707 and 750 MPa would violate the prediction without falsifying the hypothesis.
